scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

First, the sister is 21 and in her third year of university, working to support herself. She's in business school, which she finds challenging but manageable. She's been saving money from her paychecks, sometimes as much as 15% and other times as low as 1%, to fund a big vacation after she graduates. The fund currently has $2,800, and she plans to use it for a cruise, Japan, or a trip to Europe. She expects to graduate in two years. Her brother is 30, living with their parents, and is in a tough job while trying to go back to school. He's been living with them for about a year and a half. He hasn't been on a vacation in many years and has hinted that he needs one. Their parents suggested he could start saving now, maybe for a trip across the country in a year. The brother then asked the sister if he could borrow her vacation money to go to Japan this summer or fall, reasoning that she won't need it for another two years, giving him enough time to pay her back. The sister refused, citing her brother's poor money management. He makes about the same as her but is always broke, despite not paying rent or buying groceries (the sister buys most of her own groceries, makeup, health supplies, phone, and uni fees). The brother is upset, arguing that it's unfair because as the youngest, she got to go on more trips with their parents while he had to work or go to college. He also mentions that she knew what she wanted for university from the start, unlike him, and that her savings are due to being spoiled by their parents. The sister disagrees, attributing her financial skills to her father and her university classes, not spoiling. Now, the question is whether the sister is acting appropriately (AITA) by refusing to lend her brother the money. Let me consider the factors: 1. **Financial Responsibility**: The sister has been saving diligently for her future vacation, which is a significant goal. She's managed to save $2,800 despite sometimes only saving 1% of her income. Her brother, on the other hand, has a history of poor money management, always seeming broke despite earning a similar amount. 2. **Brother's Situation**: He's in a tough job, going back to school, and hasn't been on a vacation in years. He's living with their parents, not contributing to rent or groceries, which allows him to save less. However, he's asking to borrow money for a trip, which is a non-essential expense. 3. **Parents' Input**: The parents suggested he start saving now, implying they don't support him borrowing from his sister. They also mentioned that the sister's savings are a result of her own efforts, not spoiling. 4. **Emotional Arguments**: The brother is upset, bringing up past inequalities, such as the sister getting more trips as a child and him having to work or go to college earlier. He feels it's unfair that she's able to save while he struggles. 5. **Potential for Repayment**: The sister doubts her brother's ability to repay the loan in time, especially since he's already struggling financially. If he can't repay, it could strain their relationship further. 6. **Impact on Sister's Goals**: Lending the money could delay or prevent her from achieving her planned vacation, which is a reward for her hard work and savings. Considering all these points, the sister's refusal seems justified. She has a clear financial plan, and her brother's track record suggests he might not be able to repay the loan. Additionally, the vacation is a personal goal she's been working towards, and it's reasonable for her to prioritize that. The brother's arguments about fairness are emotional and don't necessarily address the financial realities of the situation. The parents' suggestion that he start saving now also supports the idea that he should handle his own finances rather than relying on his sister. Therefore, the sister is not acting inappropriately by refusing the loan. Her decision is based on practical financial considerations and the potential risks involved in lending money to someone who may not be able to repay it.
